```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)
pal <- c(navy = "#2b3a67", teal = "#2a9d8f", orange = "#e76f51",
         gold = "#e9c46a", grey = "#bbbbbb")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 15))

res <- "results"
person <- read_csv(file.path(res, "scores_per_person.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
models <- read_csv(file.path(res, "model_comparison.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, c("microbiome only", "host only", "both")))
rocs <- read_csv(file.path(res, "roc_curves.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, c("microbiome only", "host only", "both")))
auc_of <- function(m) sprintf("%.2f", models$auc[models$model == m])
mcol <- c(`microbiome only` = pal[["teal"]], `host only` = pal[["orange"]], both = pal[["navy"]])
```

## Four days, two tables, separately {.center}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 3.6
tribble(
  ~day, ~what, ~tbl,
  "Tue AM", "shape, depth, filtering", "both",
  "Tue PM", "differential testing", "both",
  "Wed PM", "distances and ordination", "both",
  "Thu PM", "sets and enrichment", "both"
) |>
  mutate(x = row_number()) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, 1)) +
  geom_tile(fill = pal[["navy"]], width = 0.9, height = 0.7, colour = "white", linewidth = 2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(day, "\n", what)), colour = "white", size = 4.3,
            lineheight = 1) +
  theme_void()
```

Every method we ran, we ran twice. Never once on both at the same time.

## Today's question {.center}

Does putting the two tables together tell you anything that neither told you
alone?

. . .

The honest answer is: **sometimes**. And you can find out which.

## When combining helps, and when it cannot {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- If both tables carry the **same** information, combining them adds nothing.
  You get a slightly better estimate of one thing.
- If they carry **different** information, combining them can add a lot.
- If one carries **nothing**, combining them makes your model worse, because you
  spent degrees of freedom on noise.
:::

. . .

So the first thing to measure is not a fancy model. It is how much the two
tables already agree.

## One number per person, from each table {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
# from the species table: how anaerobic is this person, on average
micro_score <- per_sample |>
  group_by(participant_id) |>
  summarise(micro = mean(1 - lacto_fraction))

# from the gene table: how inflamed, using Thursday's gene set
host_score <- per_sample |>
  group_by(participant_id) |>
  summarise(host = mean(inflammatory_score))
```

Two tables with 14,446 rows between them, reduced to two columns.

## How much do they agree?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(person, aes(micro_score, host_score)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = outcome), size = 2.6, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "grey40", linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(preterm = pal[["orange"]], term = pal[["navy"]])) +
  labs(x = "mean anaerobe fraction, from the species table",
       y = "mean inflammatory score,\nfrom the gene table", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Correlation: **`r sprintf("%.2f", cor(person$micro_score, person$host_score))`**.

## Which is the best possible news {.center}

The two tables are telling us about **different** things.

. . .

A disturbed bacterial community and an inflamed epithelium are not the same
measurement here, and knowing one tells you almost nothing about the other.

. . .

So each has something to add.

## Three models {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
glm(preterm ~ micro_z,           data = per_person, family = binomial)
glm(preterm ~ host_z,            data = per_person, family = binomial)
glm(preterm ~ micro_z + host_z,  data = per_person, family = binomial)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
models |>
  transmute(model,
            AUC = sprintf("%.2f", auc),
            `95% interval` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", auc_lo, auc_hi),
            AIC = round(aic)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")
```

## The picture

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5.2
ggplot(rocs, aes(fpr, tpr, colour = model)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey75", linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = mcol) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "false positive rate", y = "true positive rate", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

## What integration bought {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- Species table alone: AUC `r auc_of("microbiome only")`
- Gene table alone: AUC `r auc_of("host only")`
- Both: AUC `r auc_of("both")`
:::

. . .

Adding the host score to the microbiome model:
p = `r format(models$lrt_p_vs_micro[models$model == "both"], digits = 2)`.

. . .

That is the whole argument for multiomics, in one table, with two columns.

## And now the thing you must not forget {.smaller}

On Tuesday, preterm versus term gave **1,698 significant genes**.

. . .

Today, those same genes predict the outcome with an AUC of
`r auc_of("host only")`.

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- Significance answers "is there a difference in this group".
- AUC answers "can you tell which person is which".
- A great many small differences give you the first and not the second.
:::

## So: what is your goal? {.smaller}

The method follows from the goal, not the other way round.

| if you want to | you need |
|---|---|
| improve a prediction | a model with features from both tables |
| find features that move together | correlation across tables |
| find shared sample structure | a joint ordination |
| describe a mechanism | something more than either |

: {tbl-colwidths="[45,55]"}

## The ladder of methods {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
**Simple.** Reduce each table to a few numbers and put them in one model. What
we just did. Interpretable, cheap, and the baseline everything else must beat.

**Intermediate.** Canonical correlation, partial least squares, sparse PLS. Find
the combination of features in table A that best tracks a combination in table B.

**Multi-block.** DIABLO, MOFA. Decompose several tables at once into shared and
table-specific factors.

**Similarity-based.** Procrustes, co-inertia, DiSTATIS. Compare the sample
configurations rather than the features.

**Networks.** Build a graph across data types and look at its structure.
:::

## What each one costs you {.smaller}

| | gives you | costs you |
|---|---|---|
| scores in one model | interpretability | you chose the scores by hand |
| sparse PLS | feature pairs | tuning, and unstable selection |
| DIABLO, MOFA | shared factors | sample size, and hard-to-explain factors |
| Procrustes | one agreement statistic | no features, no prediction |
| networks | a picture | almost unlimited freedom to fool yourself |

: {tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

## The failure mode of all of them {.center}

With 157 people and 14,446 features, you can find a combination that separates
your groups perfectly.

. . .

It will not replicate.

. . .

Every method on that list needs cross-validation or a held-out set, and the
fancier the method the more it needs it.

## Our own result, honestly stated {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- We chose both scores **after** looking at the data all week.
- We never held out a test set.
- AUC `r auc_of("both")` with a 95% interval of
  `r sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", models$auc_lo[models$model == "both"], models$auc_hi[models$model == "both"])`.
- The two intervals for the single-table models overlap each other.
:::

. . .

The improvement is real and the confidence we should have in its size is modest.
Say both.
